title: Guided Journal: What It Is + 40 Free Prompts
description: What a guided journal is, how it works, who it suits, and 40 free guided journal prompts for daily, gratitude, self discovery and goal pages to use today.
h1: Guided journal: what it is, how to use it, and free prompts
intro: A guided journal is a journal with prompts or questions already on each page, so you know exactly what to write. Instead of a blank page, you answer a question like "What made you smile today?" It is the easiest way to start journaling, and you can make your own for free with the prompts below.

writer.title: What made me smile today?
writer.hint: Answer the question in a few lines. There is no wrong answer.

blocks.p: A guided journal gives you a structure to follow. Each page has a prompt, a few questions, or a simple layout to fill in. Some are themed, like gratitude, anxiety, faith, or self discovery. Others mix daily questions with weekly check-ins.
Compare that to a blank journal, where you decide everything yourself:

head: Guided journal
Blank journal
rows: Beginners, busy people, anyone who gets stuck
People who already know what they want to write

blocks.p: Many people start with a guided journal, then move to a blank one once the habit is strong. Others stay with guided pages for years because they like the focus.

ul: **Daily guided journal:** the same few questions every day, like mood, gratitude and one goal. See our [daily journal](/daily-journal/).
**Gratitude journal:** asks for good things each day. See our [gratitude journal](/gratitude-journal/).
**Self discovery journal:** deep questions about your values, past and dreams.
**Mental health journal:** gentle check-ins about feelings and self-care.
**Prayer or Bible journal:** a verse, reflection questions and a prayer. See [prayer journal](/prayer-journal/) and [Bible journal](/bible-journal/).
**Five year or line a day journal:** one short question per day, repeated each year. See [one line a day journal](/one-line-a-day-journal/).

sections.h2: Is a guided journal right for you?

blocks.p: A guided journal suits some people better than others. Here is an honest look.

blocks.h3: A guided journal is a great fit if you

ul: Freeze in front of a blank page
Have tried journaling before and quit
Only have five minutes a day
Want help with one area, like gratitude, anxiety, faith or goals
Like answering questions more than writing freely

blocks.h3: A blank journal may suit you better if you

ul: Already know what you want to write
Find set questions boring or limiting
Need space for whatever is on your mind today, not what the page asks

blocks.p: Many people keep both: a guided page on busy days and free writing when there is more to say. If a prompt does not fit your day, write what you need to instead. The guide is there to help, not to box you in.

sections.h2: How to use a guided journal

steps.name: Pick a theme
steps.text: Choose what you want help with: calm, gratitude, goals, faith, or knowing yourself better.

steps.name: Answer one prompt at a time
steps.text: Read the question, take a breath, and write the first honest answer that comes. Do not overthink.

steps.name: Skip prompts that do not fit
steps.text: You do not have to answer every question. Come back to hard ones later or not at all.

steps.name: Write a little past the question
steps.text: If an answer leads somewhere else, follow it. The prompt is a starting point, not a box.

steps.name: Keep a set time
steps.text: Five minutes with your morning drink or before bed is enough to build the habit.

example.label: Guided journal page
example.title: What made me smile today?
example.text:
A toddler on the train waving at every single person.
He waved at me three times. I waved back every time.
I forget how much small things like that lift me.
I want to notice more of them.

sections.h2: What is inside a guided journal

blocks.p: Guided journals you buy, and the ones you make yourself, usually include some of these parts:

head: Part
What it does
Example
rows: Quick mood, sleep or energy rating
Builds a habit of noticing good things
A short line at the top
A blank box or a few lines

blocks.p: When you choose or make a guided journal, look for prompts that sound like questions you would really want to answer. Avoid ones that feel preachy or too long. Short pages you finish beat long pages you dread.

example.label: Weekly review page
example.title: My week
example.text:
Best moment: swimming with the kids on Saturday.
Hardest moment: the late shift on Thursday.
Habit I kept: reading before bed, 5 nights.
One thing to change: pack lunch the night before.
Next week I am looking forward to: Jo's birthday.

sections.h2: Make your own free guided journal

blocks.p: You do not need to buy a guided journal. You can make one in a few minutes:

ol: Choose five to eight prompts from the list above that you want to answer often.
Write them at the top of each page in a notebook, or keep them in a note you read before writing.
Add a date line and a mood rating.
Once a week, add one deeper prompt from the self discovery section.

blocks.p: Prefer something ready to fill in? Try our [journal template](/journal-template/) or [printable journal pages](/printable-journal-pages/). You can also tap the **Write** button next to any prompt above to load it into the diary at the top of this page.

faq.a: A guided journal is a journal with prompts, questions or simple layouts on each page that tell you what to write about. It removes the blank page problem and gives each entry a focus. Guided journals come in many themes, including gratitude, mental health, faith and self discovery.

faq.q: Are guided journals good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. Guided journals are one of the easiest ways to start because you always know what to write. A single question is less scary than an empty page. Many beginners use guided prompts for a few months, then try free writing once the habit feels natural.

faq.q: What is the difference between a guided journal and a regular journal?
faq.a: A regular journal has blank or lined pages and you decide what to write. A guided journal gives you prompts or a structure on each page. Guided journals offer focus and ease. Regular journals offer total freedom.

faq.q: How do you use a guided journal?
faq.a: Pick a time each day, read the prompt, and write your honest answer. Skip prompts that do not fit you. If your answer leads to new thoughts, keep writing. Five to ten minutes a day is enough. Reread older pages now and then to see how you have changed.

faq.q: Can I make my own guided journal?
faq.a: Yes. Choose a handful of prompts you like, write them at the top of each page in any notebook, and add a date line. You can also use a free online journal and paste a prompt at the top of each entry.

faq.q: What should I look for in a guided journal?
faq.a: Look for a theme that matches what you want, such as gratitude, mental health, faith or goals. Check that the prompts feel natural and that the pages are short enough to finish in a few minutes. Some space for free writing is helpful. If you are not sure, try a free guided journal first by using a list of prompts.
